statement: Production AI agents should be engineered as full runtime systems whose behavior depends on the surrounding harness, not only on prompts or model weights.
A production-grade agent harness needs to govern tools, memory, verification, cost and context budgets, observability, supply-chain trust, and evaluation together as one execution envelope.
Empirical comparisons indicate that changing only the harness can move task success by large margins while holding the model fixed.

statement: A local coding-agent harness must govern what the model can see, which tools it can call, where it can write, how failures are detected, how memory persists, how cost is bounded, and how sessions can be audited.
Changing the harness can materially change long-horizon agent success even when the underlying model is held constant.
Local-agent policy should be implemented in deterministic, verifiable, monotonically constraining layers rather than relying on the model to remember rules.
The supply-chain layer should verify local agent binaries, MCP servers, dependencies, model packages, and skill packages before their outputs are trusted.
Telemetry should capture plans, tool calls, tool outputs, context decisions, and environment state while the session is running.
Project policy and context should live in version-controlled manifest files rather than only in transient prompt text.
Governance should enforce structural least privilege by withholding unneeded capabilities from the current work node.
Verification should use the LLM to draft candidate specs, tests, or explanations, but should rely on deterministic or independent checks to decide whether work is acceptable.
Harness evaluations should hold the model and runtime constant when measuring changes to manifests, tools, permissions, or verification gates.
Repository memory should promote only lessons that are structured, causally useful, and retrievable by tools.
Harness evolution should occur under rollback, held-out tasks, and formal or deterministic guards.
A good local-agent output requires behavioral correctness, maintainable structure, policy compliance, and traceable process evidence.
Repositories that allow agent edits should require agents to work on feature branches rather than directly on the protected main branch.
The project manifest should record the local agent runtime, version, model family, and execution mode used by agents.
A grounding manifest should define non-negotiable constraints, default conventions, data classes, and deterministic enforcement hooks.
An agent policy manifest should specify the success definition, quality rubric, scope boundary, data classification, quality gate, and cost policy for the repository.
Runtime-specific overlays may specialize shared project policy but must not relax the shared policy.
exception: When an overlay conflicts with a higher-level shared policy, the higher-level constraint should prevail.

statement: Agent execution should run inside a sandbox where host secrets are absent or mounted read-only.
The tool graph should separate read, search, edit, and execute capabilities so planning nodes cannot run shell commands.
Agent sessions should persist append-only logs so later reviewers can replay or diagnose the run.
The minimum verification gate should include formatting or linting, tests, secret scanning, SAST, dependency scanning, and domain invariants.
A maintainability gate should be able to fail a behavior-correct patch when structural quality is poor.

A local evaluation suite should include realistic prompts, hidden edge checks, fail-to-pass and pass-to-pass tests, manifest regressions, and ambiguity cases where the correct behavior is to ask or stop.
Agent-authored pull requests should be protected by required CI and human review.
Agent policy should define explicit token, wall-clock, command, and human-review budgets, plus compaction triggers.
Incident procedures should define how to stop work, quarantine changes, revert, rotate secrets, and replay traces.
A repository is ready for local-agent use only when sandboxing, policy inspectability, write controls, verification, auditability, manifest review, and AI-readiness checks are in place.
condition: For repositories where local agents may edit source code

statement: Manifest precedence should flow from durable hard constraints to project policy, runtime overlays, reusable skills, and finally the session plan; lower layers may specialize but not weaken higher layers.
A skill should be promoted into long-term memory only when it encodes a reusable procedure tied to observable outcomes.
condition: When deciding what belongs in a skill file rather than ordinary prose memory

statement: A session plan should record inputs, non-goals, assumptions, allowed files, allowed commands, success checks, and decisions before edits begin.
condition: When the local CLI does not provide an equivalent native planning surface

statement: Prompt files, manifest files, MCP tool descriptions, and hook policies should have regression tests because prompt-like artifacts can silently change behavior.
Manifest regression suites should assert deterministic traces, generated files, refusal or clarification decisions, and checklist completion rather than relying only on free-form prose.
Permission modes should follow a deny-first ladder, with all-permissions bypass modes avoided and never used in CI or shared repositories.
exception: Emergency local experimentation still should not bypass controls in CI or shared repositories.

statement: Capabilities beyond read, search, edit, and execute should be exposed through explicitly scoped adapters instead of broad ambient access.
Commit capability should remain unavailable until all required verification gates have passed.
The sandbox baseline should constrain filesystem writes, network access, process resources, secret injection, package installation, and protected branch writes.
External tool output should be treated as untrusted input until it has been parsed and validated.
Before seeing test results, the agent should document the intended behavior change, expected file changes, representative cases, predicted effects, known risks, and invariants.
condition: When using the DryRUN verification pattern

statement: If actual behavior diverges from DryRUN predictions, the agent should repair the work or explain the mismatch before commit.
condition: When using the DryRUN verification pattern

statement: High-risk code changes should add domain-specific guards such as state-machine invariants, schema compatibility checks, authorization tests, or formal safety properties.
condition: When the changed code is safety-, security-, workflow-, schema-, or authorization-sensitive

statement: Production-derived local evaluations should be built from real development sessions by filtering testable prompts, hiding the accepted solution, selecting relevant tests, removing flaky cases, running under a recorded harness condition, and refreshing stale tasks.
Evaluation tasks should preserve the user’s original prompt when privacy allows.
condition: When the evaluation is not explicitly testing issue-style task handling

statement: The accepted solution diff should be hidden from the agent environment during evaluation.
Local coding-agent evaluations should include both fail-to-pass tests and pass-to-pass regression tests.
Selected evaluation tests should be checked for relevance to the changed code and re-run enough to exclude flaky or environment-dependent cases.
Evaluation suites should be refreshed periodically so tasks remain aligned with current repository conventions and model training cutoffs.
Before ambitious local-agent work, the repository should be scored for agent configuration, documentation, CI/CD quality, code structure, and security.
A readiness improvement PR should add missing agent config, docs, checks, and scans before asking agents to implement product features.
condition: When repository AI-readiness gaps are found

statement: Pass-at-one should not be used as the sole reliability signal for a local coding-agent harness.
Public tests should not be the only acceptance signal because they can miss behavioral and security non-compliance.
Model leaderboard rank should not be treated as evidence that the local harness is reliable.
Agent self-rating should not be used as the final quality signal for local-agent work.
Memory-augmented local-agent systems can underperform plain long context unless stored memories are causal, structured, and retrievable by tools.
A lesson should be promoted to durable memory only when it has a concrete trigger, a procedure or invariant, an observable acceptance test, a rollback path, and an owner.
Session JSONL should record session start metadata, tool calls, tool results, verification events, and human decisions.
Multi-agent workflows should track artifact ownership states so agents do not overwrite each other or act on stale views.
condition: When multiple agents or subagents operate on related artifacts

statement: Exact project facts, current state, relations, deletions, negative queries, and explicit unknowns should be stored as schema-grounded records rather than authoritative prose memory.
Project-memory writes should validate each field against a schema and should not infer missing required facts.
condition: When storing durable project memory records

statement: Project-memory records should preserve source links, explicit unknowns, and rejected options, and memory updates should be reviewable like code.
Project-memory reads should query validated records rather than relying on LLM inference over prose summaries.
condition: When answering exact project-fact questions from memory

statement: A project-memory record should be promoted into a manifest or skill only after it proves durable across tasks.
Cost and context management should be treated as a correctness and operations requirement because unmanaged long-session context can grow quadratically.
Agent policy should define budgets for turns, tokens, tool calls, wall-clock time, network use, command classes, and human escalation.
Token warning thresholds, review counts, suite sizes, and similar numeric limits should be presented as local policy choices unless inherited from an empirical benchmark or source report.

Compaction should proceed in stages: surface budget pressure, retain only relevant output ranges, prune resolved dead ends, compact repeated tool traces, and checkpoint before restart near hard limits.

Cache policy should allow stable dependency docs and generated summaries only when permitted, prefer narrow symbol or file search over whole-repository reads, and prohibit caching secrets or red-class data.
Retrieved memory should be treated as evidence to re-validate before edits, not as unquestioned truth.

A spec-first production-change workflow should check project constraints, plan before editing, use scoped edit permissions, run verification, run local evaluation if the harness changed, and open a PR with trace evidence.
condition: For user-facing behavior, schema changes, security-sensitive code, or large refactors

statement: A test-first bug-fix workflow should reproduce the bug with a failing test or fixture, keep edits to implementation and related tests, verify the failing and neighboring tests, and promote recurring patterns only after review.

A safe refactor workflow should characterize existing behavior, freeze public interfaces, scope edit tools, run invariants and public-output checks, and reject behavior changes unless they were approved.

A dependency-update workflow should inspect changelogs and advisories, update lockfiles in a sandbox, run tests and security/license scans, record transitive changes, and require review before allowing postinstall scripts.

A documentation-only workflow should state target files, preserve wiki-link syntax when present, avoid generated or unrelated artifacts, validate Markdown structure when tooling exists, and report changed documents.

Harness evolution should be attempted only for recurring task underperformance, should vary one harness variable with the model fixed, and should keep changes only when held-out tasks show improved reliability, cost, or safety without new regressions.
condition: When changing manifests, tool scope, verification gates, compaction policy, or skills

statement: Prompt and tool-description updates should specify required and forbidden behavior with examples, add visible and hidden tests, add semantic policy mutations, run the manifest regression suite, and include rollback evidence.

When an agent enters a loop, the operator should stop the session, save the trace and diff, identify the missing tool, bad output, ambiguity, or stale context, restart from a compacted checkpoint with narrower tools, and add a detector if it recurs.
condition: When repeated calls, repeated failures without changes, context growth without evidence, or plan oscillation appears

statement: When an agent writes outside scope, the operator should stop and freeze the tree, inspect the diff and trace, revert only out-of-scope agent changes, tighten allowlists and permission mode, and add a regression or audit rule.
condition: When out-of-scope writes are detected

statement: When secret or private data is exposed, the operator should quarantine logs and artifacts, rotate exposed credentials, remove secrets from history only through approved organizational process, patch controls, and run a trace-based review.
condition: When a secret or private data exposure occurs

statement: When verification fails but the agent asserts correctness, external verification should remain authoritative; the operator should compare predictions to actual outputs, add valid mismatches as regressions, fix faulty verifiers separately, and avoid merging on agent confidence alone.
condition: When deterministic or independent verification fails

statement: When cost or context exceeds the hard budget, the session should stop, summarize plan, evidence, open questions, and current diff, then restart with minimal context or split the task if the issue recurs.
condition: When a hard cost or context cap is reached

statement: Supply-chain alerts should block merge until the affected dependency, tool, skill, or MCP server is identified, verified through provenance evidence, rebuilt in a clean sandbox, and linked to the PR and session trace.
condition: When a dependency, tool, skill, or MCP server triggers a supply-chain alert
